units.title: Genesis
units.subtitle: Stories of beginnings: creation, the first families, the ancestors

lessons.title: Creation (1): In the beginning
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Rashi on Genesis 1:1, Bereshit Rabbah 12:15, and the scholars' two-source view. Compare with your CCAR Torah commentaries.

cards.title: A first sentence with two readings
cards.body: The Torah's first word, **B'reishit**, is usually read "In the beginning." But its grammar is unusual. In the 11th century, **Rashi** argued it means "at the beginning of": the first verse sets a scene rather than naming the very first thing made. That is why the translation you'll see opens "When God began to create."

cards.q: In this account, what is the first thing God speaks into being?
cards.why: In verse 3, God says "Let there be light." Read Rashi's way, verse 1 only sets the scene, so light is the first thing spoken into being. Read the older way ("In the beginning God created heaven and earth"), heaven and earth come first. Both readings are ancient.

cards.gloss: "Unformed and void" (Genesis 1:2): the shapeless state before God brings order. In modern Hebrew, **tohu vavohu** still means a total mess.

cards.title: Spaces, then what fills them
cards.body: Read the six days as two columns. Days 1 to 3 **make spaces**. Days 4 to 6 **fill them**, in the same order.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 214' role='img' aria-label='Days 1 to 3 beside days 4 to 6' font-family='Source Sans 3, system-ui, sans-serif' font-size='13' fill='currentColor'><text x='80' y='14' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>Spaces</text><text x='240' y='14' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>Fillers</text><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-opacity='.35'><rect x='4' y='24' width='152' height='56' rx='10'/><rect x='164' y='24' width='152' height='56' rx='10'/><rect x='4' y='88' width='152' height='56' rx='10'/><rect x='164' y='88' width='152' height='56' rx='10'/><rect x='4' y='152' width='152' height='56' rx='10'/><rect x='164' y='152' width='152' height='56' rx='10'/></g><g font-weight='600'><text x='16' y='46'>Day 1</text><text x='176' y='46'>Day 4</text><text x='16' y='110'>Day 2</text><text x='176' y='110'>Day 5</text><text x='16' y='174'>Day 3</text><text x='176' y='174'>Day 6</text></g><text x='16' y='66'>Light and darkness</text><text x='176' y='66'>Sun, moon, stars</text><text x='16' y='130'>Sky and waters</text><text x='176' y='130'>Birds and fish</text><text x='16' y='194'>Dry land, plants</text><text x='176' y='194'>Animals, humans</text></svg>

src.note: "Spaces and fillers" is a common modern teaching reading of the chapter's structure; the pairs themselves are in the text.

cards.q: Day 4 fills the space made on which day?
cards.why: Day 1 makes light and darkness. Day 4 fills them with sun, moon and stars, which rule day and night.
wrong_why: The lights are set in day 2's sky (1:17), so it's a fair guess. But what they fill is day 1: light and darkness.
Day 3 comes right before day 4, so it feels next in line. It pairs with day 6: land, then the creatures that live on it.
Day 6 is a filling day too. It fills day 3's land.

cards.title: Creation, told twice
cards.body: Genesis 2 tells creation again, differently. In chapter 1, **Elohim** speaks and the world appears over seven days, with humans last. In chapter 2, God is called by the Name **YHVH**, a human is formed from soil first, then a garden, animals, and finally a woman. Most Bible scholars read the chapters as **two sources woven together**: the Priestly source (chapter 1) and a non-Priestly source (chapter 2).

src.note: Mainstream academic Bible scholarship (the source or documentary hypothesis). Your CCAR Torah commentaries are a good place to check this.

cards.title: Two names, two qualities
cards.body: The rabbis read the two names as one teaching. In a midrash, God reasons: a world made only with **justice** could not survive human failings, and a world made only with **compassion** would let wrongdoing grow. So God made it with both, which the rabbis heard in the double name "YHVH Elohim" (Genesis 2:4). In rabbinic reading, Elohim stands for justice and YHVH for compassion.

cards.q: In Genesis 2, humans are created last, after the animals.
cards.why: In chapter 2, the human is formed from the soil first (2:7). The garden, the animals and then the woman follow. Humans come last only in chapter 1.
wrong_why: That's chapter 1's order, and it's the one most people remember.

cards.q: Put the filling days in order, day 4 to day 6.
cards.why: They fill the spaces in the order the spaces were made: light, then sky and waters, then land.

cards.q: Why do most Bible scholars think Genesis has two creation stories?
choices: Two older sources were woven into one book
A scribe copied the story twice by mistake
cards.why: The chapters differ in order, style and the name for God, the marks of two separate sources joined together.
wrong_why: A copying slip would repeat the same words. These two stories differ in order, style and the name for God.
Both chapters are in the Torah text itself, centuries older than the rabbis. The rabbis interpreted them; they didn't write them.

cards.body: Every Friday night, the **Ma'ariv Aravim** blessing praises God who creates day and night and rolls light away before darkness. That is day 1 of this chapter, turned into prayer.

points: Rashi reads the first verse as setting a scene: "When God began to create."
Days 1 to 3 **make spaces**; days 4 to 6 **fill them**.
Genesis 2 tells creation again. Scholars see **two sources**; the rabbis hear two qualities of God, justice and compassion.

lessons.title: Creation (2): God's image and the seventh day
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Rashi on Genesis 1:26 and Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5. CBB's siddur (p. 42) has Vay'chulu in Hebrew inside the Friday night Amidah; it has no Kiddush section.

cards.title: A change of voice
cards.body: For five days God speaks and things appear: "Let there be." On day six the voice changes: **"Let us make"** humankind. Who is "us"? **Rashi** says God consulted the heavenly court before making humans, to teach humility: even the greatest should consult others before acting.

cards.q: After making humans, how does God describe the whole of creation?
cards.why: On the earlier days God sees that each thing is good. Only at the end of day six, looking at everything together, the text says **very good**, tov me'od (Genesis 1:31).

cards.gloss: "In the image of God" (Genesis 1:27). Every human being, male and female, bears the divine image. A great deal of Jewish ethics is built on this one phrase.

cards.title: One person, a whole world
cards.body: The Mishnah asks why God began with a single human. Its answers: so that **destroying one life counts as destroying a whole world, and saving one life as saving a whole world**; so no one can say "my ancestor was greater than yours"; and to show God's greatness. A human mint stamps coins that all look alike, but God stamps every person from the first human's seal, and **no two are the same**.

src.note: Many printed editions read "a single life of Israel"; older manuscripts read "a single life."

cards.q: Why, says the Mishnah, did God begin with a single human?
choices: To teach that each life is worth a whole world
Because the first human didn't need anyone else
To show that humans rule over the animals
cards.why: One person stands for all humanity, so each life carries the weight of a whole world, and no family line outranks another.
wrong_why: The Mishnah is making a point about worth and equality, not self-sufficiency. Genesis 2 even says it is not good for the human to be alone (2:18).
Ruling the animals is in the verse (1:26), but it isn't the Mishnah's reason for starting with one person.

cards.gloss: "And [God] ceased" (Genesis 2:2). Same root as **Shabbat** (ש־ב־ת). The word is about stopping more than relaxing.

cards.q: Vayishbot (2:2) shares a root with Shabbat. What does it mainly mean?
cards.why: Shavat means to stop or cease. Shabbat is first of all a stop: the work ends, and holy time begins.
wrong_why: Rest can sound like sleep, but the verb is about stopping work, and in the Bible God does not sleep (Psalm 121:4).
Shabbat is full of prayer today, but the verb itself only means stopping.
Shabbat is joyful, but the root means to cease.

cards.body: Genesis 2:1-3 is **Vay'chulu**. On Friday night it is said in the service, and it opens the Kiddush, so every Shabbat begins by retelling the seventh day. You're learning both in the app.

cards.title: A Reform reading
cards.body: Early on, Reform Judaism held that the creation story need not compete with science. The 1885 **Pittsburgh Platform** called modern scientific discovery "not antagonistic" to Judaism. A Reform reading asks what the story teaches: the world is ordered and good, every person bears God's image, and **time itself can be holy**. Abraham Joshua Heschel pointed out that the first thing the Torah calls holy is not a place but a day.

src.note: Pittsburgh Platform (1885), adopted by the rabbis who later founded the CCAR. A. J. Heschel, The Sabbath (1951).

cards.q: The first thing the Torah calls holy is a place.
cards.why: It's a day: God blesses the seventh day and makes it holy (2:3). Heschel built his book The Sabbath on this.
wrong_why: Later the Torah makes places holy, like Sinai and the Mishkan, so a place feels likely.

cards.q: Because every person is stamped from one "seal," the Mishnah says all people are alike.
cards.why: The point is the opposite: a human mint makes identical coins, but every person God stamps from the first human's seal is different.
wrong_why: A seal usually makes copies, which is exactly the twist the Mishnah wants you to notice.

cards.prompt: The Mishnah says each person is a whole world. Who did you see that way this week, or find it hard to?

points: Humans, male and female, are made **b'tzelem Elohim**, in God's image.
The Mishnah: one life is a whole world, and no two people are alike.
Shabbat begins as God's **stopping** (vayishbot), and the first holy thing is time.
**Vay'chulu** (Genesis 2:1-3) opens Shabbat every Friday night.

lessons.title: Garden of Eden (1): Earth, work and a partner
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Kohelet Rabbah 7:13, Rashi on Genesis 2:18 and Bereshit Rabbah 8:1. Translit of l'ovdah ul'shomrah (kamatz katan).

cards.title: A second beginning
cards.body: Genesis 1 sees the whole cosmos from far away. Genesis 2 comes in close: **one human, one garden, one job**, and a problem God notices: being alone.

cards.q: Genesis 2:15 gives the human a task in the garden. What is it?
choices: To work it and guard it
To guard the tree of life
cards.why: God places the human in the garden **l'ovdah ul'shomrah**, to work it and to guard it. Paradise comes with a job.

cards.gloss: "Human." Made from the **adamah**, the ground (2:7). In Genesis 2-3 it is mostly *ha-adam*, "the human," a title more than a name: an earthling made of earth.

cards.q: The word adam (human) is tied in the text to which word?
cards.why: The verse makes the pun itself: God forms **ha-adam** from the dust of the **adamah** (2:7), and later says the human will return to it (3:19).
wrong_why: Adom (red) shares the letters, and some later readers make that link, but the verse ties adam to the ground.
Here it is mostly ha-adam, "the human," with "the." It works more like a title than a personal name.
Dam (blood) also shares letters, but the text never makes that connection.

cards.gloss: "To work it and to guard it" (2:15). **Avad** also means to serve, as in *avodah*, worship. **Shamar** means to guard or keep, the verb of **V'shamru**: keep the Shabbat.

cards.title: No one to fix it after you
cards.body: A midrash says God led the first human around the trees of the garden: "See how beautiful and fine my works are. All of it I made for you. **Take care not to spoil and destroy my world, because if you spoil it, there is no one to repair it after you.**"

cards.q: In the midrash, why does God show the first human the trees?
choices: To warn that if the world is ruined, no one will repair it
To let the human choose which tree to eat from
cards.why: The tour ends with a warning: this world is beautiful, it is in your care, and **no one will repair it after you**.
wrong_why: The forbidden tree comes in the next verses (2:16-17), but the midrash is about caring for the whole world.
Naming comes later (2:19-20), and it is the animals, not the trees.

cards.gloss: "A helper opposite him" (2:18). **Ezer** is not a junior word: the Bible uses it for God, "my help comes from Adonai" (Psalm 121:2). **K'negdo** means facing him, his match.

cards.title: Help, or against?
cards.body: *K'negdo* can also mean "against him." **Rashi** takes both: if he is worthy, she is a help; if not, she stands against him. A midrash goes further: the first human was made **two-faced, male and female in one**, and God divided it into two. That is one reason the Contemporary Torah says God took one of his **sides** (2:21).

src.note: Also Bereshit Rabbah 8:1 (the two-faced first human).

cards.q: Elsewhere in the Bible, who is most often called an ezer, a help?
cards.why: Most often **God**: "My help (ezri) comes from Adonai" (Psalm 121:2). So ezer means strength that rescues, not a lower rank.
wrong_why: English "helper" can sound like an assistant, which is the reading the Hebrew pushes against.
Animals are brought to the human in 2:19-20, but none of them turns out to be an ezer k'negdo.
Children are never the main use of the word.

cards.body: **Shamar**, to guard, is the verb of V'shamru, which you know from Friday night: guarding the garden and keeping Shabbat use one word. On **Tu BiShvat**, the new year of the trees, many congregations, Reform ones too, read l'ovdah ul'shomrah as a call to care for the earth.

points: **Adam** (human) is made from the **adamah** (ground).
The human's task: **l'ovdah ul'shomrah**, to work and guard the garden.
Midrash: if you ruin the world, **no one will repair it after you**.
**Ezer k'negdo**: a help who faces you, a word the Bible also uses for God.

lessons.title: Garden of Eden (2): The fruit and the question
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Berakhot 40a, Rashi on Genesis 3:9, the Shneur Zalman story (as told by Buber), Berakhot 60b and Bereshit Rabbah 9:7. The original-sin card simplifies Christian teaching; check the framing.

cards.title: Not an apple
cards.body: The Torah never names the fruit. The rabbis guessed: **grapes, wheat, or a fig** (fig leaves are right there in 3:7). The apple came later, in European art and in a Latin pun: *malum* means both "apple" and "evil."

cards.q: What fruit does the Torah say grew on the tree of knowledge?
cards.why: It only says **the fruit of the tree**. Every named fruit is a later guess.

cards.q: The rabbis of the Talmud all agree the fruit was a fig.
cards.why: They disagree: Rabbi Meir says grapes, Rabbi Yehudah wheat, Rabbi Nechemiah a fig. The Torah leaves room, and they fill it in different ways.
wrong_why: The fig has a good case, since the couple sew fig leaves right after (3:7), but it is one opinion of three.

cards.gloss: "Where are you?" (3:9). God's first question to a human in the Torah, asked right after they hide.

cards.title: A question for everyone
cards.body: Rashi says God knew where Adam was and asked **to open a conversation gently**. A Hasidic story goes further. Jailed in St. Petersburg, Rabbi **Shneur Zalman of Liadi** was asked by an official why God would need to ask. His answer: in every age God calls to every person, **"Where are you in your world?"** Your years are passing; how far have you come?

src.note: Story as told by Martin Buber, The Way of Man (1948).

cards.q: In the Hasidic story, why does God ask "Where are you?"
choices: It asks every person to take stock of their life
God had lost track of Adam
To catch Adam in a lie
cards.why: The question isn't about location. It asks each person to **take stock**: where am I in my life, and where am I going?
wrong_why: Rashi says plainly that God knew where Adam was.
Some readers do see the question as giving Adam room to own up, but the story turns it into a question for every person, not a trap.

cards.title: No original sin
cards.body: Christian teaching, especially from **Augustine** (around 400 CE), holds that Adam's sin passes to every person. Judaism never made that a doctrine. The story brings real consequences: work, pain, death. But each morning's prayer says: **"My God, the soul you placed in me is pure."** A few rabbinic passages speak of a lasting stain, but it never became Jewish teaching.

src.note: Elohai n'shamah, from the morning blessings. The stain: Shabbat 146a.

cards.q: In mainstream Jewish teaching, every person is born carrying Adam and Eve's sin.
cards.why: The morning prayer **Elohai n'shamah** says the soul in each of us is **pure**. People sin, but no one inherits guilt.
wrong_why: That is the Christian doctrine of original sin, so it's easy to assume the story means the same in Judaism.

cards.title: The "evil" urge is very good
cards.body: The rabbis speak of two drives: the **yetzer tov** (good inclination) and the **yetzer hara** (evil inclination). A midrash reads Genesis 1:31, "very good," as including the yetzer hara: **without it, no one would build a house, marry, have children, or go into business.** Desire isn't the enemy; it needs direction.

cards.q: Why, says the midrash, does "very good" include the yetzer hara?
choices: Without it, no one would build, marry or have children
Because humans can always overcome it
cards.why: The same drive that can lead to wrong also **builds houses and families**. The goal is to direct it, not destroy it.
wrong_why: The midrash treats it as part of the world God called very good, not a mistake.
The midrash says it is needed, not that people overcome it.

cards.body: The story ends with the way to the **tree of life** guarded by cherubim and a fiery sword (3:24). When the Torah scroll goes back into the ark, the congregation sings **Etz chayim hi**: "It is a tree of life to those who hold it" (Proverbs 3:18). The tree is out of reach, but Torah is offered in its place. The Torah service lessons will come later.

cards.prompt: Ayekah, where are you? If the question came to you today, how would you answer?

points: The Torah never names the fruit; the rabbis guess grapes, wheat or a fig.
**Ayekah**, "Where are you?": a question for every person, in every age.
Judaism has **no original sin**: the soul in each of us is pure.
The **yetzer hara** is part of what is "very good": it builds, if it's directed.
**Etz chayim hi**: Torah as a tree of life.

lessons.title: Cain and Abel (1): The offerings and the door
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Rashi on Genesis 4:3 and Bereshit Rabbah 22:7. Claim to check: chatat (4:7) is the Torah's first word for sin.

cards.title: Two names
cards.body: Eve names her first son **Kayin**: "I have gained (*kaniti*) a man with God" (4:1). The second son gets no explanation, but his name says plenty: **Hevel** means breath or vapor, the word Ecclesiastes uses for "vanity" (*havel havalim*). He passes like a breath.

cards.q: Why does God accept Abel's offering and not Cain's?
cards.why: The text gives **no reason**. It only describes what each brought, and readers have been filling the gap ever since.

cards.title: Reading the gap
cards.body: Look at the details. Abel brings **the firstlings of his flock and their fat**, the best. Cain brings just "from the fruit of the soil." **Rashi** says Cain brought the worst of his crop. Care, not the kind of gift, makes the difference.

cards.q: According to Rashi, why was Cain's offering not accepted?
choices: He brought the worst of his crop
He brought it on the wrong day
cards.why: Rashi reads "from the fruit of the soil" as **the worst of it**, set against Abel's firstlings and best portions.
wrong_why: Later the Torah has grain offerings, also called *minchah* (Leviticus 2), so plants weren't the problem.
The text says only "in the course of time"; nothing about the day.

cards.gloss: "Sin crouches at the door" (4:7), like an animal waiting. The word **chatat**, sin, appears here for the first time in the Torah: not in the Garden, but just before the first murder.
"And you can rule over it" (4:7). Sin wants Cain, but **the choice is his**. John Steinbeck built *East of Eden* around this one word.

cards.q: In 4:7, what does God tell Cain about sin?
choices: It is waiting, but you can master it
You are already doomed to it
cards.why: Sin is **waiting at the door**, but Cain **can master it**. The verse puts the choice in his hands.
wrong_why: The verse says the opposite: v'atah timshol bo, you can rule over it.
The serpent is from the Garden; this verse never mentions it.
God points Cain to how he acts, not to a ritual.

cards.title: The missing words
cards.body: "Cain said to his brother Abel..." and then **nothing**. The Hebrew leaves his words out (the Contemporary Torah prints "…"). The midrash fills the silence with arguments: over **dividing the world**, over **whose land the Temple would stand on**, over **a woman**. Every version is a fight about having more.

src.note: The Septuagint and the Samaritan Torah add "Let us go out to the field."

cards.q: Genesis 4:8 tells us what Cain said to Abel.
cards.why: It doesn't. The verse says "Cain said to his brother Abel" and **breaks off**. The midrash and some ancient translations fill the gap.
wrong_why: Some ancient translations add "Let us go out to the field," so you may have read a version that has words there.

cards.body: "You can rule over it" is the idea behind **t'shuvah**, turning back: Judaism assumes you can always choose again. You met the same idea in the Garden lesson: the **yetzer hara** is a drive to steer, not a fate.

cards.q: What does the Torah say Abel brought?
choices: The choicest firstlings of his flock
cards.why: **The choicest of the firstlings of his flock** (4:4), the best he had.
wrong_why: That is Cain's offering (4:3).
Bread and wine come later, with Malki-tzedek (Genesis 14:18).

cards.prompt: Sin crouches at the door, yet you can master it. When has something waited at your door, and what helped you master it?

points: **Kayin** (gained) and **Hevel** (breath).
The Torah never says why Abel's offering was accepted; Rashi points to Cain's careless gift.
**Chatat**, sin, first appears at Cain's door, and **timshol**: you can rule over it.
4:8 breaks off; the midrash fills the silence with fights over having more.

lessons.title: Cain and Abel (2): The keeper and the cry
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, Rashi on Genesis 4:13 and Bereshit Rabbah 22:13. The shomer link to Eden is my reading.

cards.title: Where is your brother?
cards.body: In the Garden God asked Adam **"Where are you?"** Now God asks Cain **"Where is your brother?"** Adam hid; Cain lies, and answers with a question of his own.

cards.q: Who puts a mark on Cain, and why?
cards.why: God marks Cain **so that no one who meets him will kill him** (4:15). The "mark of Cain" is protection, not a brand.

cards.gloss: "Am I my brother's keeper?" (4:9). **Shomer**, keeper, is the root of *l'shomrah*: the first human was put in the garden to **guard** it. One chapter later, Cain refuses to guard his brother.

cards.q: Shomer (keeper) shares its root with which word from the Garden of Eden lessons?
cards.why: **L'shomrah**, to guard it (2:15). Same root, ש־מ־ר: guarding the garden, keeping Shabbat (V'shamru), and the brother Cain won't keep.
wrong_why: Shabbat's root is ש־ב־ת (to stop), a different word.
Shalom's root is ש־ל־ם (whole).
Sh'ma's root is ש־מ־ע (hear).

cards.gloss: "Your brother's **bloods**" (4:10). The Hebrew is plural; English translations usually say "blood."

cards.title: Bloods, not blood
cards.body: The Mishnah notices the plural: **his blood and the blood of all the descendants he would have had.** It is the same passage you met in Creation: whoever destroys one life destroys a whole world. Judges read it to witnesses in a capital case, so they would feel the weight of a life.

src.note: It also offers a second reading: his blood was spattered on trees and stones.

cards.q: What lesson does the Mishnah draw from "bloods"?
choices: Killing one person destroys a whole future world
A murderer must be punished twice
Blood can never be washed away
cards.why: Abel's **whole future line** died with him. Killing one person destroys a whole world.
wrong_why: The Mishnah isn't about punishment here; it is about what was lost.
Nothing in the passage says this; the plural points to the people who never lived.

cards.title: Punishment, or sin?
cards.body: **Avon** means both sin and its punishment, so Cain's words can mean "my punishment is too great to bear" or "my **sin** is too great to bear." **Rashi** hears a question: You carry the heavens and the earth, and You can't carry my sin? God answers with a **mark that protects** him.

cards.q: The mark of Cain was a sign of shame, so others would reject him.
cards.why: God puts the mark on Cain **"lest anyone who met him should kill him"** (4:15). It protects him.
wrong_why: "Mark of Cain" became an English phrase for disgrace, so the shame reading feels natural.

cards.title: Cain meets Adam
cards.body: A midrash: Adam meets Cain and asks how his judgment went. Cain says, **"I did t'shuvah, and it was settled."** Adam strikes his own face: "Such is the power of t'shuvah, and I didn't know!" Right away he sings **"Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbat: tov l'hodot ladonai,"** reading *l'hodot* as both "to give thanks" and "to confess."

cards.q: In the midrash, why does Adam sing Psalm 92?
choices: He learns from Cain how powerful t'shuvah is
To mourn that Abel was at fault
cards.why: Cain's story shows him **the power of t'shuvah**, and Adam answers with "It is good to give thanks (and confess) to God."
wrong_why: It's Shabbat's psalm, but in this midrash it comes from what Adam learns from Cain.
Nothing in the midrash blames Abel.

cards.body: You know **Mizmor Shir** from Kabbalat Shabbat. Next Friday night, when you reach *tov l'hodot*, you're singing the line the midrash gives Adam after hearing Cain.

points: "Where is your brother?": Cain answers **"Am I my brother's keeper (shomer)?"**, the root of guarding the garden.
**D'mei**, bloods: one life holds a whole future world.
**Avon**: sin and punishment; the mark **protects** Cain.
Midrash: Adam learns the power of t'shuvah from Cain and sings **Psalm 92**.

lessons.title: Noah (1): Righteous in his generation
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Rashi on Genesis 6:9 and 6:13 (Sanhedrin 108a). The tevah-as-word teaching: I attribute it to the Baal Shem Tov but am not sure of the exact book; please check.

cards.title: A grieving God
cards.body: The flood story doesn't open with anger. It opens with **regret and grief**: God "regretted having made humankind" and was pained **to the heart** (6:6). The destruction comes from a broken heart.

cards.q: What does the Torah name as the earth's crime before the flood?
cards.why: Twice the Torah says the earth was **filled with chamas** (6:11, 6:13): violence, lawlessness, people taking what isn't theirs.

cards.gloss: "Lawlessness, violence" (6:11). **Rashi** says it means **robbery**. The Talmud adds that the flood generation did every kind of wrong, but their fate was **sealed by robbery**: everyday stealing from one another.

cards.q: According to Rashi, what sealed the flood generation's fate?
choices: Robbery, people taking from each other
cards.why: **Robbery** (chamas). They did many wrongs, but taking from each other is what the Talmud says sealed the decree.
wrong_why: Rashi says they did that too, but it isn't what sealed the decree.
The Torah never says Noah prayed for them; that silence comes up later in this lesson.

cards.title: Righteous, compared to whom?
cards.body: "Blameless **in his generation**" (*b'dorotav*). The rabbis split. Some read it as **praise**: if he was righteous among such people, how much more in a good age. Others read it as a **limit**: next to his neighbors he looked righteous; next to Abraham he would have counted for little.

cards.q: How can "righteous in his generation" be read as a limit?
choices: He looked righteous only next to a wicked generation
He became righteous only in old age
cards.why: Read as a limit: he was righteous **only by his generation's low standard**. The other reading takes the same words as praise.
wrong_why: B'dorotav is about the people around him, not how long he lived.
Nothing in the verse is about his age.

cards.title: Noah doesn't argue
cards.body: Noah does **everything he is told** (6:22) and says **nothing** on behalf of the world. Compare Abraham, who hears Sodom will be destroyed and pushes back: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth deal justly?" (18:25). Jewish teachers often set the two side by side: obedience is not the whole of righteousness.

src.note: My comparison; a common one in Jewish teaching.

cards.gloss: "Ark." The only other place the Torah uses it: the **basket** that carried baby Moses (Exodus 2:3). In later Hebrew tevah also means "**word**," and a Hasidic teaching reads "come into the tevah" as: **enter the words of your prayer**.

src.ref: Teaching attributed to the Baal Shem Tov

cards.q: Where else in the Torah does the word tevah appear?
choices: The basket that carried baby Moses
cards.why: In **Moses' basket** (Exodus 2:3). Both times, a small vessel carries life through water.
wrong_why: The Ark of the Covenant is an *aron*, a different word.
The Tabernacle is the *mishkan*.

cards.body: Try the Hasidic reading next time you pray: treat each word as a **tevah**, a small shelter to step inside. Start with the two lines of **Barchu**.

points: The flood begins with God's **grief**.
The crime is **chamas**; Rashi: robbery sealed the decree.
**B'dorotav**: praise, or righteous only by a low standard.
Noah obeys but never argues for the world; Abraham will.
**Tevah**: the ark, Moses' basket, and in later Hebrew a word of prayer.

lessons.title: Noah (2): The bow in the clouds
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Sanhedrin 56a, Tosefta Sanhedrin 13:2, Ramban on Genesis 9:12, Berakhot 59a and Chagigah 16a. Please check the Ramban card most closely.

cards.title: Same reason, opposite answer
cards.body: Before the flood, God sees that every human thought is "only evil" (6:5). After it, God says nearly the same thing, the human heart "is evil from youth" (8:21), and then promises **never again**. The diagnosis hasn't changed. The response has.

cards.q: Why does God promise never to flood the earth again?
choices: Because human hearts lean toward evil from youth
Because Noah proved humans are good
Because the flood washed evil away
cards.why: Surprisingly, it's **the same reason** given for the flood: humans lean toward evil. This time God chooses patience.

cards.gloss: "The devising of the human heart" (8:21). **Yetzer** here is where the rabbis' **yetzer hara**, the drive you met in the Garden lessons, gets its name.

cards.q: After the flood, God promises mercy because humans have become good.
cards.why: The verse says the opposite: the human heart is **evil from youth**, and God promises anyway.
wrong_why: It would make sense for a promise to follow improvement, but here it doesn't.

cards.title: Laws for everyone
cards.body: After the flood God gives laws to **all humanity**, and the first protects human life, "for in the image of God was humankind made." The rabbis count **seven laws for the children of Noah**: set up courts, and do not curse God, worship idols, commit sexual wrongs, murder, rob, or eat a limb torn from a living animal.

cards.gloss: "Children of Noah": every human being. A rabbinic teaching holds that **the righteous of all nations have a share in the world to come**; you don't have to be Jewish to be righteous.

cards.q: Why do the rabbis speak of laws for the "children of Noah"?
choices: Everyone descends from Noah, so they are laws for all humanity
Only Noah's own family had to keep them
They replaced the Torah for Jews
cards.why: Everyone alive descends from Noah, so these are **laws for all humanity**, and anyone who keeps them is righteous.
wrong_why: "Children of Noah" means everyone, not one family.
They were never meant to replace the Torah for Jews; they are a shared baseline for all people.

cards.gloss: "Bow," the same word as a **war bow**. **Ramban** notes the rainbow is set with no arrow and its ends turned **down toward the earth**, the way a warrior hangs up a bow: a sign that God is not shooting at us.

cards.title: A blessing for rainbows
cards.body: When you see a rainbow, the Talmud gives a blessing: *Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha-olam,* **zocher habrit, v'ne-eman bivrito, v'kayam b'ma-amaro**: who **remembers the covenant**, is faithful to it, and keeps God's word. Some also say not to stare at a rainbow for long, out of awe.

cards.q: What does the rainbow blessing praise God for?
cards.why: **Remembering the covenant** (zocher habrit) and keeping the promise of Genesis 9.
wrong_why: The blessing is about the promise, not the weather.
It is about the covenant, not the colors.

cards.q: Which word in Genesis 8:21 gives the rabbis the name yetzer hara?
cards.why: **Yetzer**, the devising or drive of the human heart.
wrong_why: Keshet is the bow in chapter 9.
Chamas is the lawlessness before the flood.
Tevah is the ark.

points: Before and after the flood, the same diagnosis: the human heart leans toward evil. After, God chooses **patience**.
**Yetzer** (8:21) is where the yetzer hara gets its name.
**Seven laws for the children of Noah**: a moral baseline for all humanity.
**Keshet**: a bow hung up, not aimed. Blessing: **zocher habrit**.

lessons.title: The Tower of Babel
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 24, Rashi on Genesis 11:5 and the Netziv (Ha'amek Davar on Genesis 11:4; please check this one most closely). Bab-ili etymology: standard scholarly view.

cards.title: One language, one plan
cards.body: "Everyone on earth had **the same language and the same words**" (11:1). Humanity is finally united, and what it decides to do with that unity is build a tower **to make a name for itself**.

cards.q: What does the Torah say was wrong with building the tower?
cards.why: The Torah **never names the sin**. It gives their motives, a name for themselves and fear of being scattered, and leaves the judgment to the reader.

cards.gloss: "Let us make a name for ourselves" (11:4). One chapter later God tells Abram the opposite way round: **"I will make your name great"** (12:2). A name you grab, or a name you're given.

cards.title: A brick worth more than a person
cards.body: A midrash pictures the work: the tower grew so tall that hauling bricks up took a year. **If a person fell and died, no one noticed. If a brick fell, they wept**: when will another one come up in its place?

cards.q: In the midrash, what shows the builders had lost their way?
choices: They mourned a fallen brick more than a fallen person
They used brick instead of stone
The tower took a whole year to climb
cards.why: They **mourned a fallen brick more than a fallen person**. The project mattered more than the people building it.
wrong_why: The midrash doesn't fault the bricks; what's wrong is what they cared about.
Height makes the work slow, but the point is how they treated the workers.

cards.title: God came down to see
cards.body: Why would God need to **come down to look**? **Rashi**: God didn't need to. The verse teaches judges **not to rule until they have seen for themselves**.

cards.q: Rashi asks why God had to "come down to look." What is his answer?
choices: To teach judges to see for themselves before ruling
Because God couldn't see from heaven
cards.why: It's a lesson for human judges: **see for yourself before you rule**.
wrong_why: Rashi says plainly God didn't need to come down to know.
The verse is about looking, not about stopping the work by force.

cards.gloss: **Bavel**, Babylon. The Torah makes a pun: there God **balal**, confused, their speech. In Babylon's own language the name meant "**gate of the god**" (Bab-ili), and its great stepped temple-tower likely stands behind the story.

src.note: Akkadian Bab-ili; the ziggurat Etemenanki in Babylon.

cards.q: The Torah links the name Bavel to which Hebrew word?
cards.why: **Balal**, confused or mixed up: "there God confused the speech of the whole earth" (11:9).
wrong_why: Bab-ili, gate of the god, is what the name meant in Babylon's language; the Torah turns it into a pun about confusion.
Levenah (brick) appears in the story, but the verse ties the name to balal.

cards.title: The danger of one voice
cards.body: The **Netziv** (19th-century Lithuania) reads "the same words" as **enforced sameness**: a society afraid of anyone leaving or thinking differently. Scattering them into many languages wasn't only a punishment; it **restored room to differ**, and fulfilled God's charge to fill the earth (9:1).

src.note: Netziv, Rabbi Naftali Tzvi Yehudah Berlin.

cards.body: Aleinu, which you know, ends with a different kind of unity: **"On that day Adonai will be one, and God's name will be one"** (Zechariah 14:9). Not one human name made great, and not one language forced on all, but **many peoples** recognizing one God.

points: One language, one plan: **"Let us make a name for ourselves."**
The Torah never names the sin; a midrash: **a brick mattered more than a person**.
Rashi: God "came down to see" so judges would **see before they rule**.
**Bavel / balal**: Babylon becomes "confusion."
Netziv: the danger was **forced sameness**; scattering restored difference.

lessons.title: Abraham and Sarah (1): Go forth
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Rashi on Genesis 12:1 and 12:5, Bereshit Rabbah 39:1, Berakhot 13a and Pesachim 117b (all read on Sefaria 11/09). Building 'lit up' vs 'on fire': translations differ.

cards.title: Go, without a map
cards.body: God's first words to **Abram** are a command: **leave** your land, your birthplace and your father's house, for "the land that **I will show you**" (12:1). No destination is named.

cards.q: Why does the Torah say God chose Abram?
choices: He won an argument with his father
cards.why: The Torah **gives no reason**. The midrash fills the gap, as you'll see.

cards.gloss: **Lech l'cha**, literally "go, to you." Why the extra word? **Rashi**: go **for your own benefit and your own good**.
**Veh'yeh b'rachah**, "and you shall be a blessing" (12:2). Not only blessed: **a blessing for others**. The next verse widens it to all the families of the earth.

cards.title: The lit-up building
cards.body: **Rabbi Yitzchak**'s parable: a traveler sees a building **lit up** (some translate: on fire) and wonders, does this place have **no one in charge**? The owner looks out: **I am the owner.** So Abraham looked at the world and asked, and God answered him.

cards.q: In the parable, what does the traveler do before the owner speaks?
choices: He asks whether the building has an owner
cards.why: He **asks the question**: does this place have someone in charge? Then the owner answers.
wrong_why: Nothing in the parable has him fight the fire: he wonders and asks.
The point is that he **stops and asks**.

cards.title: The souls they made
cards.body: Abram and Sarai set out with "the persons they had acquired in Haran" (12:5). **Rashi** quotes a midrash: these are people they brought **under the wings of the Shechinah**. **Abraham taught the men and Sarah taught the women**, and the Torah counts it as if they had made them. (Rashi adds the plain sense: their servants.)

cards.gloss: **Anochi magen lach**, "I am a shield to you" (15:1). The Amidah's first blessing ends **Magen Avraham**, shield of Abraham. The Talmud reads 12:2's "you shall be a blessing" as that very ending: **the blessing concludes with you**.

**Av hamon goyim**, "father of a multitude of nations" (17:5): Abram becomes **Abraham**, and Sarai becomes **Sarah** (17:15). The Talmud: Abram was a father to Aram, Abraham to the whole world. Sarai, "my princess," was a princess to her own people; Sarah, to everyone.

cards.q: In Berakhot 13a, what do the new names mean?
choices: Their role grows from one people to the whole world
They were given new names to hide from enemies
cards.why: Abram, father to **Aram**, becomes Abraham, father to **all**; Sarai, princess to **her people**, becomes Sarah, princess to **all**.
wrong_why: Nothing in the text points to hiding.
Terach is not part of this explanation.

cards.body: In the Amidah you already know: **Elohei Avraham ... Elohei Sarah**, and the ending **magein Avraham v'ezrat Sarah**. The shield of 15:1 and the blessing of 12:2 are in that line.

cards.prompt: Abram left before he knew where he was going. When have you started something before you knew where it led?

points: **Lech l'cha**: go, with no destination named; Rashi: for your own good.
**Veh'yeh b'rachah**: be a blessing for others.
Midrash: the **lit-up building** and its owner.
Rashi: Abraham taught the men, **Sarah the women**.
**Magen Avraham** (15:1, Pesachim 117b) and the new names (Berakhot 13a).

lessons.title: Abraham and Sarah (2): The tent and the laughter
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Shabbat 127a, Rashi on Genesis 18:13, Bava Metzia 87a, Megillah 31a, Rosh Hashanah 11a (read on Sefaria 11/09). Which Torah reading CBB uses on Rosh Hashanah: not checked.

cards.title: A hot afternoon
cards.body: Abraham sits at the **entrance of his tent** in the heat of the day (18:1). He looks up, sees **three strangers**, and **runs** to greet them.

cards.q: When they arrive, the Torah tells us the three visitors are angels.
cards.why: The Hebrew calls them **anashim**, men ("three figures" in this translation). Abraham greets them as travelers.

cards.title: Guests before God
cards.body: The chapter opens with **God appearing** to Abraham, then the guests arrive. **Rav**: welcoming guests is **greater than receiving the Divine Presence**, since Abraham asked God to wait ("do not go on past your servant," 18:3) while he ran to them.

cards.gloss: **Al na ta'avor me'al avdecha**, "please do not go on past your servant" (18:3). Said to the guests, or, as Rav reads it, **to God**.

cards.q: Why does Rav say hospitality is greater than receiving the Divine Presence?
choices: Abraham asked God to wait while he served his guests
Abraham never saw God that day
cards.why: Rav reads 18:3 as Abraham **asking God to wait** while he ran to the strangers.
wrong_why: Rav's point is the opposite: God and the guests are different, and the guests came first.
The chapter begins with God appearing to him (18:1).

cards.title: Changed for peace
cards.body: Sarah laughs: "with **my husband** so old?" (18:12). Reporting it to Abraham, God quotes her as "old as **I** am" (18:13). **Rashi**: the words were changed **for the sake of peace** between them. The Talmud: peace is so great that even God altered the truth for it.

cards.q: What did God change when telling Abraham about Sarah's laugh?
choices: "My husband is old" became "I am old"
God left out that she laughed
cards.why: Sarah's words about **Abraham's** age became words about **her own**, to keep peace in the home.
wrong_why: God does mention the laugh: "Why did Sarah laugh?" (18:13).
Nothing like that is in the text.

cards.gloss: **Hashofeit kol ha'aretz lo ya'aseh mishpat?** "Shall not the Judge of all the earth deal justly?" (18:25). Abraham **argues with God** for strangers in Sodom. Noah, told of the flood, said nothing.

cards.q: What does Abraham do when God tells him about Sodom?
cards.why: He **steps forward and argues**: will You sweep away the innocent with the guilty? (18:23)
wrong_why: That was Noah. Abraham speaks up.
The Torah shows him arguing with God, not traveling.

cards.gloss: **Tz'chok asah li Elohim**, "God has brought me laughter" (21:6). Her son is named **Yitzchak**, Isaac, from the same root: laughter.

cards.body: The Talmud teaches that **Sarah was remembered on Rosh Hashanah** (Rosh Hashanah 11a), and gives Genesis 21, "Adonai took note of Sarah," as a Rosh Hashanah Torah reading (Megillah 31a). Check what your congregation reads.

points: Abraham **runs** to three strangers in the heat (18:1-2).
Rav: guests **before** the Divine Presence (Shabbat 127a).
Sarah's laugh, retold **for peace** (Rashi 18:13, Bava Metzia 87a).
**"Shall not the Judge of all the earth deal justly?"** Abraham argues.
**Yitzchak**: God brought Sarah laughter.

lessons.title: Abraham and Sarah (3): Hagar and Ishmael
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Ramban on Genesis 16:6, Rashi on Genesis 16:13 and 21:17 (read on Sefaria 11/09). 'First angel in the Torah' = first occurrence of mal'ach (16:7).

cards.title: The first to meet an angel
cards.body: The first person in the Torah to meet **a messenger of God** is not Abraham or Sarah. It is **Hagar**, Sarah's Egyptian slave, alone by a spring in the wilderness (16:7).

cards.q: Who is the first person in the Torah to meet an angel?
cards.why: **Hagar** (16:7). The word mal'ach, messenger or angel, appears here for the first time.

cards.title: Ramban doesn't excuse Sarah
cards.body: Abram tells Sarai, "Deal with her as you think right," and Sarai **treats Hagar harshly** until she runs away (16:6). **Ramban** (13th-century Spain): Sarah **did wrong** by this, and **Abraham did wrong** by allowing it. God heard Hagar's suffering.

cards.q: How does Ramban judge Sarah's treatment of Hagar?
choices: As a wrong, by Sarah and by Abraham
As fair, since Hagar was her servant
cards.why: He calls it a **transgression** by Sarah, and by Abraham for allowing it.
wrong_why: Ramban says the opposite: it was wrong.
He comments directly on 16:6.

cards.gloss: **Atah El Ro'i**, "You are El-roi," a God of seeing (16:13). Hagar names God from her own experience. Her son's name, **Yishmael**, means "God hears": "for Adonai has paid heed to your suffering" (16:11). **Rashi**: the One who sees the humiliation people suffer at others' hands.

cards.q: What do the names El-roi and Yishmael say about God?
cards.why: **El-roi**: God who sees. **Yishmael**: God hears, heeding Hagar's suffering.
wrong_why: Those aren't in either name.
Those belong to the creation story, not to Hagar.

cards.gloss: **M'tzachek**, "playing" (21:9). Years later Sarah sees Ishmael **m'tzachek** and demands that Hagar and her son be sent away. It's the same root as **Yitzchak** and Sarah's laughter. The Torah doesn't say what kind of playing it was.

cards.title: Where he is
cards.body: "God has heeded the cry of the boy **where he is**" (21:17). **Rashi**: he is judged by **what he is doing now**, not by what his descendants might do later. Rashi also notes that God heard **the boy's own voice**: a sick person's own prayer is accepted more readily than others' prayers for him.

src.note: from Rosh Hashanah 16b and Bereshit Rabbah 53:14

cards.q: In Rashi's reading of "where he is," how is Ishmael judged?
choices: By what he is doing now
By what his descendants will do
cards.why: **As he is now.** The future doesn't decide the present.
wrong_why: Rashi rejects exactly that: the angels raised it, and God answered, what is he now?
Hagar's actions aren't the basis here.

src.note: from Rosh Hashanah 16b and Bereshit Rabbah 53:14

cards.title: Together at the end
cards.body: Many years later, when Abraham dies, **"his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him"** in the cave of Machpelah (25:9). The brothers who were separated stand together at their father's grave.

cards.prompt: Hagar names God from her own experience: El-roi, the God who sees. What name would come from yours?

points: **Hagar** is the first person in the Torah to meet an angel (16:7).
Ramban: Sarah and Abraham **did wrong** by her (16:6).
**El-roi**, God who sees; **Yishmael**, God hears.
Rashi on 21:17: judged **as he is now**; a person's own prayer is heard.
Isaac and Ishmael **bury Abraham together** (25:9).

lessons.title: Abraham and Sarah (4): The binding of Isaac
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Rashi on Genesis 22:2 and 22:6 (from Sanhedrin 89b), Rosh Hashanah 16a, Megillah 31a, Ibn Ezra on Genesis 22:19 (read on Sefaria 11/09). CBB's Rosh Hashanah reading not checked.

cards.title: Here I am
cards.body: It is one of the hardest stories in the Torah. Through it runs one word: **hineni**, here I am. Abraham says it to **God** (22:1), to **Isaac** (22:7) and to the **angel** (22:11).

cards.q: How many times does Abraham answer "hineni" in this chapter?
cards.why: **Three times**: to God, to Isaac, and to the angel who stops him.

cards.title: Your son, your only one
cards.body: Why does God name Isaac so slowly? **Rashi** retells a Talmudic dialogue: God: "Your son." Abraham: "I have two sons." God: "Your only one." Abraham: "Each is the only son of his mother." God: "Whom you love." Abraham: "I love them both." God: "Isaac."

cards.gloss: **Hineni**, here I am. Not a place but **readiness**: I'm listening, I'm present. The same word answers God, a son and an angel.
**Vayelchu sh'neihem yachdav**, "the two walked off together" (22:6), said again in 22:8. **Rashi**: Abraham, who knew what was coming, walked with the same willingness as Isaac, who did not.
**Elohim yir'eh lo haseh**, "God will see to the sheep" (22:8): Abraham's answer to Isaac's question. The same verb, **to see**, names the place afterward: **Adonai yireh** (22:14).

cards.title: The ram and the shofar
cards.body: Abraham looks up and sees **a ram caught by its horns** (22:13), and offers it instead of his son. **Rabbi Abbahu**: that's why the Rosh Hashanah shofar is a **ram's horn**. God says: blow it before Me, and I will **remember the binding of Isaac**.

cards.q: According to Rosh Hashanah 16a, why is the shofar a ram's horn?
choices: To recall the ram offered instead of Isaac
Rams were the only animals with horns
Abraham blew it on the mountain
cards.why: God says: sound a ram's horn, and **I will remember the binding of Isaac** for you.
wrong_why: Other animals have horns too; the Talmud gives a different reason.
The Torah doesn't say Abraham blew a horn.

cards.title: Where is Isaac?
cards.body: At the end, "**Abraham** returned to his servants" (22:19). Isaac isn't mentioned. **Ibn Ezra** (12th-century Spain): he was there, in his father's care. Those who claim Isaac was actually slaughtered and revived, he says, **contradict the text**.

cards.q: How does Ibn Ezra explain why Isaac isn't named in 22:19?
choices: He was there, in Abraham's care
He had been slaughtered and revived
He had gone off on his own
cards.why: He reads Isaac as **present and safe**, and rejects the idea that he died.
wrong_why: Ibn Ezra rejects that reading as contradicting Scripture.
That isn't Ibn Ezra's explanation.

cards.body: The Talmud has this chapter read on the **second day of Rosh Hashanah**, to recall the binding on the day of judgment (Megillah 31a), and the **shofar** recalls it every year. Many congregations read it on Rosh Hashanah; check what CBB reads.

cards.prompt: Hineni means being fully present. Where in your life right now would you like to be able to say hineni?

points: **Hineni**: here I am, said to God, Isaac and the angel.
Rashi: "your son... your only one... whom you love... Isaac."
**The two walked together** (Rashi 22:6).
The ram's horn: **the shofar remembers the binding** (Rosh Hashanah 16a).
Ibn Ezra: Isaac was there, **safe**, at the end.

lessons.title: Abraham and Sarah (5): Sarah's life and the cave of Machpelah
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Rashi on Genesis 23:1, 23:2 and 23:4, Bava Metzia 87a, Bereshit Rabbah 79:7 (read on Sefaria 11/09).

cards.title: A portion called "Life"
cards.body: This Torah portion is called **Chayei Sarah**, "the life of Sarah," yet it opens with **her death** (23:1-2). Abraham comes **to mourn her and to weep for her**, then rises to find her a resting place.

cards.q: How did Abraham get the cave of Machpelah?
choices: He paid full price for it
It was a gift he accepted
He took it in a war
cards.why: Ephron offers it as a gift, but Abraham **insists on paying** 400 shekels of silver (23:16).

cards.gloss: **Sh'nei chayei Sarah**, "the years of Sarah's life" (23:1). The verse counts 100 years, 20 years and 7 years separately. **Rashi**: "years" is repeated to show that **all her years were equally good**.

cards.title: Why here?
cards.body: Sarah's death comes right after the binding of Isaac. **Rashi** quotes a midrash: when she heard that her son had been readied as an offering and nearly sacrificed, the shock was too much, and **she died**.

cards.q: Why does Rashi say the verse repeats the word "years"?
choices: To show all her years were equally good
To show she lived longer than Abraham
cards.why: The repetition tells us **every stage of her life was good**.
wrong_why: Rashi says nothing about comparing their ages.
Rashi reads it as praise, not doubt.

cards.gloss: **Ger v'toshav anochi imachem**, "I am a resident alien among you" (23:4): an outsider who has settled down. **Rashi** adds a midrash: if you sell, I'm a stranger and will pay; if not, I'll claim it as a resident, **by right**.

cards.q: What do the two words ger and toshav describe?
choices: An outsider who has settled down
cards.why: **Ger**, stranger, from another land; **toshav**, resident, settled among them. Abraham is both.
wrong_why: Neither word means king or servant.
The words describe Abraham alone.

cards.title: Say little, do much
cards.body: Ephron offers the field as a **gift**, in front of everyone (23:11). Then he names a price, 400 shekels: "what is that between you and me?" (23:15). **Rabbi Elazar**: the righteous **say little and do much**, like Abraham running to his guests; the wicked **say much and don't do even a little**, like Ephron.

cards.title: Paid in full
cards.body: Abraham **weighs out the silver** in public (23:16) and buries Sarah in the cave of Machpelah (23:19). A midrash: Machpelah is one of **three places** no one can call stolen, because they were bought: the cave of Machpelah, the Temple site and Joseph's tomb.

cards.q: Why does the midrash stress that Machpelah was paid for?
choices: So no one can say it was stolen
cards.why: It's one of three places **bought outright**, so no one can claim it was taken.
wrong_why: Ephron did offer a gift; Abraham chose to pay.
Nothing in the text says Ephron was poor.

cards.prompt: Abraham mourns, and then rises to do what has to be done (23:3). What helps you move between grieving and doing? It's fine to skip this one.

points: **Chayei Sarah**, the life of Sarah, opens with her death.
Rashi: **all her years were equally good**.
**Ger v'toshav**: an outsider who has settled down.
Bava Metzia 87a: **say little, do much** (Abraham, not Ephron).
Machpelah was **paid for**, never taken (Bereshit Rabbah 79:7).

lessons.title: Abraham and Sarah (6): Rebekah at the well
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Rashi on Genesis 24:14, 24:57 and 24:67, Berakhot 26b (read on Sefaria 11/09). Ten camels: Genesis 24:10.

cards.title: A test of kindness
cards.body: Abraham sends his servant to find a wife for Isaac. At a well, the servant prays for a sign: the young woman who offers water **to him and to his camels** (24:12-14).

cards.q: What sign does the servant ask God for?
choices: A woman who offers water to him and his camels
The most beautiful woman at the well
A woman who knows Abraham's name
cards.why: The sign is **kindness beyond what's asked**: water for a stranger, and for his camels too.

cards.gloss: **Va'aseh chesed**, "deal graciously" (24:12). **Chesed**, loving-kindness, is this chapter's key word: the servant asks God for chesed, and looks for a woman who shows it. **Rashi**: if she is fitting, "I'll know You have shown kindness to my master."

cards.title: She ran
cards.body: Count Rebekah's verbs: she **hurries**, lowers her jar, gives him drink, empties it, **runs** back to the well, and draws for **all** his camels (24:18-20). He had ten camels (24:10). She does far more than she was asked.

cards.q: What made Rebekah the answer to the servant's prayer?
choices: She offered water to his camels too, without being asked
She asked who his master was
cards.why: His sign was **chesed beyond the request**, and she gave it, running back again and again.
wrong_why: She was family, but that wasn't the sign he prayed for.
She didn't ask; she simply helped.

cards.gloss: **Elech**, "I will" (24:58): one word. Her family says "let us call the girl and ask her." **Rashi**: from here we learn that a woman is not married **without her own consent**.

cards.q: What does Rashi learn from "let us call the girl and ask her"?
choices: A woman is not married without her consent
A bride must travel the same day
cards.why: Asking Rebekah teaches that **her own yes** is required.
wrong_why: The verse teaches the opposite: they ask her.
The timing isn't Rashi's point.

cards.gloss: **Lasuach basadeh**, Isaac went out "walking in the field" toward evening (24:63). **Lasuach** can also mean to converse, so the Talmud reads it as **prayer**: Abraham began the morning prayer, and **Isaac began Minchah**, the afternoon prayer.

cards.q: According to Berakhot 26b, which prayer did Isaac begin?
cards.why: From "lasuach basadeh **toward evening**": Isaac's prayer is the afternoon one.
wrong_why: The Talmud credits Abraham with the morning prayer.
That isn't Isaac's; the verse says toward evening.

cards.title: Comfort after his mother
cards.body: Isaac brings Rebekah into **his mother Sarah's tent**, loves her, and is comforted after his mother (24:67). **Rashi** quotes a midrash: in Sarah's lifetime a **lamp burned** from one Shabbat eve to the next, there was **blessing in the dough** and a **cloud** over the tent. They stopped when she died, and **returned with Rebekah**.
In the Amidah's first blessing you say **Elohei Rivkah**, God of Rebekah, right after Elohei Sarah. And every **Minchah** is, in the Talmud's reading, Isaac's walk in the field.

points: The sign: **chesed beyond the request** (24:14).
Rebekah **runs** to water ten camels.
**Elech**, "I will": Rashi, no marriage **without her consent**.
**Lasuach basadeh**: Isaac begins **Minchah** (Berakhot 26b).
Sarah's lamp, dough and cloud **return with Rebekah** (Rashi 24:67).

lessons.title: Jacob and Esau (1): Twins and the birthright
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Rashi on Genesis 25:22, 25:27 and 25:30 (with Bereshit Rabbah 63 and Bava Batra 16b), read on Sefaria 11/09. Note the Contemporary Torah renders yoshev ohalim as 'raising livestock'.

cards.title: Two in one womb
cards.body: Rebekah's twins **struggle inside her** (25:22). She asks the question people in pain ask, **why?**, and then goes **to inquire of God**.

cards.q: Rebekah keeps her distress to herself.
cards.why: She speaks it aloud and **goes to inquire of Adonai** (25:22), and God answers her.

cards.gloss: **Lamah zeh anochi**, "why do I exist?" or "why am I like this?" (25:22). Rebekah doesn't stop at the question: she goes **lidrosh**, to seek out God.

cards.title: Running to the doors
cards.body: **Rashi** reads "struggled" as **running**: whenever Rebekah passed a house of Torah study, **Jacob** strained to come out; whenever she passed a pagan temple, **Esau** did. He also gives the plain reading: the twins **fought** with each other.

cards.q: In Rashi's midrash, why did the twins move inside Rebekah?
choices: Each was drawn to a different kind of place
They wanted to be born first
cards.why: Jacob toward **houses of study**, Esau toward **pagan temples**: two paths from the start.
wrong_why: Hunger isn't part of this midrash.
Rashi's midrash here is about where each was drawn, not birth order.

cards.gloss: **Ish tam yoshev ohalim**: this translation says "a mild man, raising livestock"; word for word, "a **whole** man, **dwelling in tents**." **Rashi**: tam means his heart matched his mouth, not clever at deceiving; the tents are the study tents of **Shem and Ever**.

cards.q: What does Rashi say tam means?
cards.why: **Tam**: whole, straightforward. What was in his heart was in his mouth.
wrong_why: Tam isn't about strength.
Tam describes character, not birth order.

cards.title: A mourner's meal
cards.body: Why was Jacob cooking lentils? **Rashi**: **Abraham died that day**, and Jacob was preparing the first meal for the mourners. Lentils are **round like a wheel**, because mourning is a wheel that comes around to everyone.

cards.gloss: **Vayivez Esav et hab'chorah**, "thus did Esau spurn the birthright" (25:34). The Torah's own verdict comes after a rush of verbs: **he ate, drank, rose and went**.

cards.q: Whom does the last line of the story judge?
choices: Jacob, for driving a hard bargain
cards.why: The verse names **Esau**: he "spurned the birthright."
wrong_why: The Torah doesn't comment on Jacob here, though readers have long argued about him.
Isaac isn't in this scene.

cards.body: Jacob is the one who **dwells in tents**. Every Shabbat morning you open with **Mah tovu ohalecha Yaakov**, "how good are your tents, Jacob" (Numbers 24:5).

points: **Lamah zeh anochi**: Rebekah's why becomes a search for God.
Rashi: the twins ran toward **study houses** and **temples**.
**Ish tam**: heart and mouth matched (Rashi 25:27).
The lentils: **a mourner's meal** for Abraham (Rashi 25:30).
**Vayivez Esav**: the Torah's verdict on the sale.

lessons.title: Jacob and Esau (2): The stolen blessing
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Rashi on Genesis 27:1, 27:19 and 27:22 (from Midrash Tanchuma) and Bereshit Rabbah 67:4, read on Sefaria 11/09.

cards.title: One blessing, two brothers
cards.body: Isaac is old and **cannot see**. He plans to bless **Esau**. Rebekah overhears, and sends **Jacob** in to take the blessing in disguise (27:1-17).

cards.q: When Isaac asks "Which of my sons are you?", what does Jacob answer?
cards.why: "**I am Esau, your first-born**" (27:19). Rashi works hard with those words, as you'll see.

cards.title: Why was Isaac blind?
cards.body: **Rashi** gives two midrashim: the **smoke** of the incense Esau's wives offered to idols dimmed his eyes; or, at the binding of Isaac, the **angels wept** and their tears fell into his eyes.

cards.title: A lie, or not quite?
cards.body: "Anochi Esav b'chorecha," I am Esau your firstborn. **Rashi** splits the sentence: "**I am** the one bringing you food" and "**Esau is** your firstborn." He reads the words so Jacob doesn't tell an outright lie.

cards.q: How does Rashi read Jacob's "I am Esau your firstborn"?
choices: As two statements: "I am the one bringing food" and "Esau is your firstborn"
As a plain lie the Torah approves
cards.why: Rashi **divides the sentence**, so each half is true.
wrong_why: Rashi tries to avoid that conclusion.
Rashi reads the Hebrew as it stands.

cards.he: הַקֹּל קוֹל יַעֲקֹב וְהַיָּדַיִם יְדֵי עֵשָׂו
cards.gloss: **Hakol kol Yaakov v'hayadayim y'dei Esav**, "the voice is the voice of Jacob, yet the hands are the hands of Esau" (27:22). **Rashi**: Jacob's voice was **gentle**, "please sit up"; Esau would speak **harshly**, "let my father sit up" (27:31).

cards.q: According to Rashi, what gave Jacob's voice away?
cards.why: Jacob said **"please"**; Esau's way of speaking was harsh.
wrong_why: Rashi is about manner, not pitch.
Rashi says nothing about languages here.

cards.gloss: **Havrachah achat hi l'cha avi?** "Have you but one blessing, Father?" (27:38). Then **Esau wept aloud**. The Torah lets us hear the pain of the brother who lost.

cards.title: The cry comes back
cards.body: **Rabbi Chanina**: Jacob caused Esau **one great and bitter cry**. It was repaid generations later in Shushan, when **Mordecai** cried out "a loud and bitter cry" (Esther 4:1). God is patient, the midrash says, but the debt is remembered.

cards.q: In Bereshit Rabbah 67:4, how was Esau's cry repaid?
choices: By Mordecai's bitter cry in Shushan
Jacob was never held to account
Esau later took the blessing back
cards.why: The same words, **a great and bitter cry**, come back in the Book of Esther.
wrong_why: The midrash says the opposite: God collects, patiently.
Nothing in the Torah says Esau took it back.

cards.prompt: Jacob is our ancestor, yet the Torah makes us hear Esau's sobbing. Why might it tell the story this way?

points: Isaac, blind, plans to bless **Esau**; Rebekah sends **Jacob**.
Rashi on 27:19: "**I am** (bringing food); **Esau is** your firstborn."
**The voice is Jacob's**: gentle, "please" (Rashi 27:22).
"**Have you but one blessing?**" Esau weeps.
Bereshit Rabbah 67:4: the cry returns as **Mordecai's**.
